newsitem.title: GERMANY: German cocoa physicals hampered by price strength.
newsitem.headline: German cocoa physicals hampered by price strength.

text.p: German cocoa sellers are meeting only patchy demand for beans and butter in a high-price period which began in the second week of June, traders said.
"It's all speculation and currency, there is no cocoa shortage," one said.
"The industry took some spot replacement cover last week and some first half 1998 supply, but that's all."
London futures in the afternoon extended gains on the back of a strong New York market and September was last up 10 stg at 1,160 stg/tonne, below the day's one-year high of 1,170.
Traders said the El Nino weather phenomenon, which was providing underlying price support, could affect Asia's cocoa growing areas.
West Africa dominates German imports, and producers there would take advantage of any Asian output shortfalls.
In the domestic market, traders believed the cocoa grind figure for the second quarter, a key demand indicator, might be unchanged to seven percent below last year's 59,471 tonnes.
They said the chocolate industry had not been reporting successful sales and the negative long-term effects of capacity shifts to elsewhere in western Europe had not yet been absorbed.
They were also sceptical about optimistic export sales projections to eastern Europe, which export promoters German Sweets published last week.
One trader said reports of sluggish Polish and Russian sales were making the rounds.
The grindings data will be released on July 7 or 8.
Second half 1997 cif beans for good West African quality were priced at 3.30 marks/kg, having gained 10 percent in June.
The cocoa butter ratio remained broadly unchanged over the last fortnight and stood at 2.39 for third quarter and 2.46 for fourth quarter delivery.
